opening.headline: When output problems repeat, we explain how to check whether the fix was really the cause by classifying cause types and checking for regression.
body: What should I do if the classification results are shaky and the problem does not go away even after adding “exactly” to the instructions, changing the temperature settings, and adding an example? If you've made multiple modifications but can't tell which modification was aimed at what, it's difficult to decide what to fix next.

In this lesson, we will divide output problems into three types of causes: lack of instructions, lack of examples, and unspecified format. Then, make corrections that fit the cause one at a time, and learn the procedure of checking the inputs that failed and the inputs that worked again after making the corrections.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the types of causes of output consistency problems
Errors can be classified into lack of instructions, lack of examples, and unspecified format.
You can determine whether the amendment fits the cause.

screens.title: The same error keeps happening and I don't know what to do to fix it.
screens.lead: Please read the revision history and output history below. I read this while thinking about why the problem remains even after I corrected it three times.

visual.alt: A scene where three revisions and five different outputs lead to a question mark.
labels: Edit 1: Added correct to instructions - still shaky.
Fix 2: Change temperature settings - only a small improvement
Edit 3: Added an example - another error occurred.

paragraphs: There are emotion classification prompts. For the same type of input, the output will be different: `positive`, `positive`, `Positive.`, `probably positive`, and the empty string. At first I added “exactly” to the instruction sentence and it still faltered. Next, I changed the temperature settings and there was only some improvement. Finally, I added an example and this time a different error occurred.

All three revisions were plausible, but hit different spots. The problem was that there was no way to check if the fix was really the cause. One symptom is “label shaking,” but there may be a mix of different causes underneath it. Empty strings and 'probably positive' appear to be the same symptoms, but have different places to fix.
So what you need to do before fixing it is to divide the symptoms by cause. This class covers the standards for dividing and the procedures for revising and checking one by one after dividing.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If the symptoms are the same, is the cause also the same? By the end of class, you will be able to answer this question with evidence.

screens.outro: First, let's think about how to usually fix output errors.

screens.title: Was the fix really the cause?
screens.lead: As you select each method, the instructor's thoughts unfold. First, think about how you usually check things and then press it. You will not enter or submit an answer.

items.prompt: After fixing it, try running the same input once more.
items.answer: This is the most common verification method. You can see if input that failed now passes. But this alone doesn't tell us whether other inputs have introduced new errors. In this lesson, we complement this approach with regression checking.

items.prompt: Retry inputs that failed in the past
items.answer: This is a step further. By running multiple inputs together, you can determine whether the modification was tailored to only one case. Verification will be complete only if successful inputs are included.

items.prompt: Classify errors by type before fixing them.
items.answer: This is the most reliable method. Splitting errors makes it clear which fix targets which cause and provides a reason to fix one at a time. This is the starting point for this class.

screens.outro: Let’s start by checking the criteria for dividing the cause.

screens.title: Three types of causes: lack of instructions, lack of examples, and lack of format.
screens.lead: Select each tab to see typical symptoms and verification questions for each cause type. It is good to note that the same symptoms can occur from any cause.

visual.alt: A flow chart showing how one symptom can be divided into three causes.

tabs.label: lack of instructions
tabs.body: Out-of-bounds responses result from vague or vague dos or don'ts rules. For example, if the instructions do not specify an acceptable label, the model may use a label such as 'neutral' that is not in the list. If you don't decide how to answer in a certain situation, an empty string may appear. The confirmation question is this: Did this response break the rule written in the instructions, or was there no rule?

tabs.label: lack of examples
tabs.body: Since it has never shown a judgment pattern, the results vary for each ambiguous input. The Gemini Guide explains that examples are often used to control form, expression, scope, and overall pattern. This includes cases where the exact shape or boundary judgment is shaky, such as the capital letter `Positive` or 'probably positive'. The confirmation question is this: Have you ever shown an example that resembles this input?

tabs.label: Format not specified
tabs.body: Since the output shape is not determined, it comes in any shape, such as a sentence, a text with an explanation, JSON, or XML. The first item in Claude's consistency guide is to precisely define the desired output format with JSON, XML, or custom templates. Responses with explanations before and after are typical examples. The confirmation question is this: Who ever said that the output should be labels only?

tabs.label: three types of relationships
tabs.body: The same symptom, “label shaking,” can occur from all three causes. So, if you only look at the symptoms and fix them, you end up affecting other areas. Diagnosis involves looking at the symptoms and asking three questions to determine the cause. Since one symptom may have two or more overlapping causes, classification must be done separately for each response.

screens.outro: Now that you know the three types, let's break down the five actual error responses.

screens.title: Sort five error responses by cause
screens.lead: Read the table from top to bottom to follow how the instructor determines the cause for each response. The Basis for Judgment column is key. Don't assume the cause as soon as you see the response; check what was written in the instructions first.

data.caption: Error response five cause classification
rows: `Affirmative. The reason is that I like the product.`
Explanations are added before and after the label.
Since we never said to just print the label, the shape is not set.
The exact label shape is not fixed in the example.
A value that is not an acceptable label was returned.
The list of acceptable labels was not in the instructions, so it was out of range.
There are no examples showing how to judge ambiguous input.
There are no instructions on how to respond in any given situation.
data.notes: All five responses can be lumped together as “labels are wobbly,” but the causes were split into one: lack of formatting, two, lack of examples, and two, lack of instructions. Even if the symptoms are the same, if the causes are different, the treatment options are also different. This is why trying to fix five things "correctly" at once didn't work. It is also noticeable that if you classify, there is a high possibility that a case of unspecified format can be resolved simply by determining the output shape.

screens.outro: Now that we have divided the causes, let’s look at the order in which to fix them and how to check them.

screens.title: Fix priorities and regression checks
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to follow the flow step by step from diagnosis to confirmation. The last step explains why regression checking is necessary.

visual.alt: A four-stage circular flow from determining the cause to recording.
labels: If you see a new error, try again

steps.title: Ways to increase consistency
steps.body: The Claude consistency guide suggests defining output formats as JSON, XML, or user templates, prefilling the response start only in supported models (using structured output/format instructions from Claude 4.6 onwards), constraining with examples, anchoring the context with searches, and splitting and linking prompts for complex tasks. The means to be used will vary depending on the type of cause.

steps.title: Priorities: First things with high impact and certainty.
steps.body: Fix things one by one, starting with those with obvious causes and the greatest impact. The order of inspection is efficient in the following order: lack of format, lack of instructions, and lack of examples. This is because if the format is not determined, it is difficult to identify other causes.

steps.title: Edit one thing at a time
steps.body: If you fix several places at once, you won't know which fix was effective. Even if some things improve, if you don't know the reason, you can't use them for the next diagnosis. Even though it may seem slow, fixing things one by one is ultimately faster.

steps.title: Check for regression
steps.body: After making corrections, run again the input that failed the first time and the input that was already working well. This is because modifications may create new errors in other inputs. If a new error is discovered, revert the previous fix or determine the cause again.

steps.title: Managing changes like code
steps.body: OpenAI recommends leaving production prompts in your code and shifting them to testing and deployment. Prompts, like code, have a history and must go through a verification process so that when a problem occurs, you can trace which change was the cause.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the procedure, let us move on to an explanation to determine whether the amendment fits the cause.

screens.title: Explanation: Which correction matches the cause?
screens.lead: Select the title of the amendment to expand it. The symptom is that the classification labels are mixed up as `positive`, `Positive`, and `positive`, and the instructor determines which cause each amendment targets.

items.title: Amendment A: Add “classify accurately” to instructions.
items.body: This correction is independent of cause. If label spellings are mixed up, it's not because the model broke a rule, but because we've never seen the correct shape. The expression “exactly” is less effective because it contains no information about shape.

items.title: Amendment B: Specify three allowed labels and output appearance, anchored by three pairs of examples
items.body: This fix is consistent with the cause. Putting an acceptance label on the instructions prevents lack of instructions, specifying the output shape prevents unformatting, and example triplets fixes correct spelling. This is the final improvement targeting the three cause types. To distinguish effects, allowable labels, output shapes, and examples should be added one by one rather than combined all at once and compared in the same evaluation set.

items.title: Amendment C: Add a rule paragraph with a longer explanation
items.body: This fix is at secondary level. Forms are communicated more clearly when shown through examples rather than explained in sentences. The Claude Consistency Guide also explains that constraints with examples are more effective than abstract instructions. If the rule paragraph is long, it may conflict with other instructions.

items.title: Instructor's judgment
items.body: Whether the modification fits the cause determines the effect. Amendment A is at odds with the cause, and Amendment C only indirectly targets the cause. Only Amendment B is directly linked to the cause. When evaluating an amendment, first ask what type of cause it is targeting.

screens.outro: Now that we've chosen an amendment, let's follow the verification process behind the amendment from start to finish.

screens.title: Explanation: Steps from correction to regression confirmation
screens.lead: Select the arrow to the right to follow your instructor as he progresses from recording symptoms to recording results.

steps.title: Step 1: Record your symptoms
steps.body: The five failed responses are classified by cause and presented in a table. If you write down the number together, such as one case where the format is not specified, two cases where there is a lack of examples, and two cases where there is a lack of instructions, it is easy to determine where to fix it first.

steps.title: Step 2 One fix
steps.body: First, we specify only the allowed labels and evaluate them with the same input. Next, add the output shape and finally an example, recording the results and regression at each step. Amendment B is the final draft that will be completed after verification.

steps.title: Step 3: Retry input failure
steps.body: Let's go back to the five that failed the first time and see if they all come up with a single word label. If one or two still fail, re-categorize the cause of the response. This is because the previous classification may have been wrong, or the two causes may have overlapped.

steps.title: Step 4: Check regression
steps.body: Re-run inputs that previously worked well to see if any new errors have occurred. Without this confirmation, it's easy to miss the problem. For example, if you started classifying even negative reviews as positive after adding examples, this will reveal itself.

steps.title: Step 5 Record
steps.body: It leaves which fix was effective for which cause. Building this record will make diagnosis much faster the next time you encounter similar symptoms. It's okay for the records to be short. Just four lines in one line are enough: symptom, cause type, correction, and result.

screens.outro: Now that we've completed the process, let's close by summarizing the main points.

screens.title: Key takeaway: Even though the symptoms are the same, the causes are different.
screens.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class. Check the answer to the question posed at the beginning: if the symptoms are the same, the cause is also the same.

paragraphs: To answer the first question, even if the symptoms are the same, the causes may be different. Lack of formatting, lack of examples, and lack of instructions all came under the one symptom of shaky labels. So attempts to fix all symptoms at once by adding “exactly” or changing temperature settings have been inconsistently effective.

Diagnosis begins with classifying the cause type by response. Lack of instructions if there is no task or acceptable range; Lack of examples if no judgment pattern or exact shape has been shown; Lack of format if the output shape has not been determined. The order of inspection is efficient in the following order: lack of format, lack of instructions, and lack of examples.

Modifications are made one at a time, and after modifications, the inputs that failed and those that worked well are run again to check for regression. Lastly, if you keep a record of what causes and what modifications were effective, you can use them for the next diagnosis. Prompts, like code, are more stable if they have change history and testing.

If you look at the first three revisions again using this procedure, the direction will already have changed from the first revision. If I had divided the symptom into five cases, I would have decided on the allowable label and output shape first instead of adding "exactly", and if I had fixed them one at a time, I would have been able to immediately attribute any new errors that appeared when I added an example to that correction. A few minutes spent on diagnosis will save you from multiple trials and errors later. The first thing to do when encountering a printing problem is not to fix it, but to share it.

callout.label: Procedure to remember
callout.text: Divide the cause, fix only one, rerun the failed input and the existing input together, and record it.

glossary.def: This is the process of finding the causes of different outputs from the same input by dividing them by type.
This is a classification that divides output problems into three categories: lack of instructions, lack of examples, and unspecified format.
The order is to fix things one at a time, starting with those with clear causes and the greatest impact.
After modification, the input that failed and the input that was already working are rerun to check whether any new problems have occurred.

misconceptions.myth: If an error occurs, you can write stronger instructions.
misconceptions.fact: If the cause is an example or format, strong language is ineffective. First, you need to determine the type of cause.

misconceptions.myth: It will be resolved faster if you fix several areas at once.
misconceptions.fact: If you fix several places at once, you won't know which fix was effective. In the end, it's faster to fix things one at a time.

misconceptions.myth: It is enough to retry only the input that failed and pass.
misconceptions.fact: Modifications may create new errors in other inputs. You need to re-run the inputs that were working well to check for regression.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Even if the symptoms are the same, the causes may be different.
The causes can be divided into lack of instructions, lack of examples, and unspecified format.
Fix one thing at a time and see what works.
After modification, the failed input and the existing input are rerun together to check for regression.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What caused the last output error I encountered?

title: Diagnosing inconsistency: instructions, examples, and formats

checks.q: The output showed 'neutral', which is not in the list of allowed labels. If there is no allowable label in the instructions, what is the proximate cause?
options: Lack of examples: No pattern of judgment has been demonstrated.
Format not specified: The output shape has not been determined.
Lack of instructions: Acceptable labels are not in the instructions.
Temperature setting is set too low
checks.explain: If the instructions or scope are vague or vague, an over-the-scope response will result. Not having a list of acceptable labels is a lack of direction.

wrong.0: Lack of examples is more a case of shaky judgment of ambiguous input.
wrong.1: Unspecified format is a matter of appearance, as is the prefix.
wrong.3: Changing the settings does not create an acceptable range.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. When you select one of the views, a commentary appears. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: After fixing the prompt, why do I restart the input that initially failed and the input that worked?
options: In order to reduce the time, it is enough to just hit the failure input.
Trying to make sure the fix didn't create a new error
To secure the amount of information by increasing the length of the response
Trying to determine the effect even if several modifications are made at once
checks.explain: Since a correction may create a new error in a different input, check for regression by re-running the input that was working well.

wrong.0: If you only look at the failure input, you will miss any new errors that have occurred.
wrong.2: The goal is not response length.
wrong.3: To mask the effect, you need to fix one thing at a time.
